PART I 01 Application Architecture Decide how the system is decomposed, how its parts communicate, how traffic reaches them, and how workflows are coordinated. 14 COMPARISONS

PART I OVERVIEW PART I I Application Architecture Part I covers the decisions you make before you choose a database or a cache: how to carve the system into deployable units, how those units talk to each other, how requests enter the system, and how multi-step workflows are coordinated. These choices are the most expensive to reverse, which is why interviewers use them to separate engineers who can name technologies from engineers who can reason about constraints. The fourteen comparisons are grouped into four questions. Decomposition (chapters 1–3, 11, 14) asks how to split the system and how to structure code inside each piece. Communication (4–7) asks whether calls are synchronous or asynchronous and which protocol carries them. The traffic edge (8–10, 13) asks what stands between clients and services. Coordination (12) asks who owns the flow of a business process that spans services. Throughout, the running example is an e-commerce platform with Spring Boot services behind an API gateway, backed by relational and NoSQL stores, Redis, and Kafka, with a standard observability stack. 01 Monolith vs Microservices Decide whether the system ships as one deployable unit or as many independently deployable services. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER A monolith ships every capability as one deployable unit, with in-process calls and usually one database. Microservices split capabilities into independently deployable services that talk over the network. Microservices buy team and release independence at the price of distributed-systems complexity. Start with a well-structured monolith; split only when team scale, divergent scaling needs, or release coupling justify the cost. Visual explanation Figure 1.1 — Left: modules call each other in-process and share one transactional database. Right: each service owns its data and every interaction crosses the network, which introduces latency and partial failure. Solid arrows are synchronous calls. Many small services, each owning one business capability and deployed independently. Architecture Modules in one process; in-process calls; typically one shared schema. Services behind a gateway; database per service; REST, gRPC, or messaging between them. Latency Method calls inside one process add negligible overhead. Each hop adds serialization, network time, and tail-latency risk; deep call chains multiply it. MONOLITH Throughput Scales by running more identical instances behind a load balancer, if the app is stateless. Scales per service, so a hot capability can get more instances without scaling the rest. Consistency modules. A single ACID transaction can span all No cross-service ACID; use sagas, outbox, and eventual consistency. Availability One bad release or memory leak can take down everything; simple failure model. Faults can be isolated with timeouts, bulkheads, and circuit breakers, but only if they are designed in; there are more failure modes. Best use cases Early products, small teams, unclear domain boundaries, strong transactional needs. Many autonomous teams, clearly bounded domains, parts with different scale or compliance profiles. Microservices make those boundaries physical with separate deployments and databases. The modular monolith keeps in-process speed and simple transactions while preserving a path to extraction. Prefer it by default; extract a module when it needs independent scaling, release cadence, or isolation. Visual explanation Figure 2.1 — Both styles share the same logical boundaries. In the modular monolith they are enforced by module visibility rules and tests; in microservices they are enforced by the network and by separate databases. 03 SOA vs Microservices Compare enterprise-wide service integration through a central bus with small, independently owned services. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER SOA organizes reusable, coarse-grained enterprise services, usually integrated through a central bus that handles routing, transformation, and policy. Microservices use small services around bounded contexts, with logic in the services and simple communication between them. The boundary is blurry because microservices grew out of service orientation. Choose by integration context: heterogeneous legacy estates lean SOA, product teams lean microservices. Visual explanation Figure 3.1 — In classic SOA the bus mediates between consumers and large shared services. In microservices the endpoints carry the logic, the pipes stay simple, and each service owns its data. Side-by-side comparison DIMENSION SOA MICROSERVICES Core concept Reusable business services exposed across the enterprise, governed centrally. Small services aligned to bounded contexts, owned by autonomous teams. Granularity Coarse: whole business functions such as “Customer” or “Billing”. Fine: a focused capability with its own data. Middleware Often an ESB doing routing, transformation, and sometimes orchestration. Smart endpoints and dumb pipes: plain HTTP, gRPC, or a simple broker; logic stays in services. SOA Contracts Typically SOAP/WSDL and WS-* standards, with a canonical data model (not mandatory, but common). REST, gRPC, or events; each service defines its own model and versions its contract. Data Often shared databases or shared enterprise data models. Database per service; no shared schema. Governance Centralized standards, registries, and reuse policy. Decentralized; teams choose within platform guardrails. Best use cases Integrating many heterogeneous, long-lived systems (mainframes, packaged ERP, partners). Building products from autonomous teams with fast, independent delivery. When should you choose soa vs microservices? CHOOSE You are building new products with autonomous teams, need independent release and scaling, MICROSERVICES and can invest in platform tooling. HYBRID Keep the integration layer around legacy systems as an anti-corruption layer and build new capabilities as microservices that call it. Do not rip out working mediation just to match a trend. 04 Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication Decide whether a caller waits for the answer or hands off work and continues. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER Synchronous communication blocks the caller until the callee responds, which gives an immediate answer and simple error handling but couples the two in time. Asynchronous communication hands off a message or event through a broker and continues, which absorbs spikes and decouples availability at the cost of eventual completion, duplicates, and harder debugging. Use sync when the answer is needed now; use async for decoupling and long-running work. Visual explanation Figure 4.1 — Left: the request thread waits through the whole chain. Right: Orders publishes an event, returns 202 Accepted, and Payments processes it later. Dashed cyan arrows are asynchronous. 05 REST vs GraphQL Choose between resource-oriented HTTP endpoints and a single typed query interface where the client shapes the response. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER REST exposes resources at URLs with fixed representations and uses HTTP semantics, which makes it simple, cacheable, and universally supported. GraphQL exposes one typed schema where clients request exactly the fields they need, reducing round trips and over-fetching but shifting complexity, caching, and cost control to the server. Choose REST for simple, cacheable APIs and GraphQL for diverse clients with varied data needs. Use gRPC for lowlatency request/response; use messaging for decoupled, bursty, or multi-consumer work. Use a plain proxy for generic web traffic; use a gateway when many clients consume your APIs and policy should be enforced once at the edge. They complement each other. Add a mesh only when many services need consistent network policy that you do not want in every codebase. 10 Server-Side vs Client-Side Load Balancing Decide whether a dedicated balancer picks the backend instance or the calling service does. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER With server-side load balancing, clients send traffic to a balancer that picks an instance and tracks health, so clients stay simple but the balancer is an extra hop and a shared dependency. With client-side load balancing, the caller fetches the instance list from a registry and chooses directly, removing the hop but putting policy and stale-data risk into every client. 15 SQL vs NoSQL Choose between a relational model with joins and rich transactions and a family of stores built around specific access patterns and horizontal scale. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER SQL databases model data as related tables with a schema, joins, and multi-row ACID transactions, and they answer ad-hoc queries well. Default to a relational database; pick NoSQL for a named access pattern or scale need it serves better. 25 Strong Consistency vs Eventual Consistency Choose between always reading the latest committed value and accepting temporary staleness for speed and availability. Use strong consistency for invariants like balances and uniqueness; use eventual consistency where brief staleness is harmless and availability or latency matters more. 32 Materialized Views vs Real-Time Querying Precompute expensive results and refresh them, or compute the answer from base data on every request. THE 30-SECOND ANSWER A materialized view stores the result of a query and refreshes it on a schedule, on demand, or incrementally, so reads are fast but data can be stale. Real-time querying runs the query against base tables each time, always current but paying the full cost per request. Use materialized views for expensive aggregates read often and tolerant of staleness; use direct queries when freshness matters or the query is cheap.
